summary:
Bremen has no trans-specific statute or ordinance of its own. The city-state operates Germany's Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz) unchanged, and the federal criminal-law framework applies without local modification.

Under that act, adults over 18 may change their legal gender by self-determination rather than through the former medical and court pathway, with the change entered in the civil registry. In Bremen the entry is processed by the city-state's own registry offices, so the local administration of the procedure is a Bremen responsibility.

Prison placement is governed the same way. Bremen has no inmate-placement statute of its own; all German states tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender, section 6(1) of the Self-Determination Act allows state law to override the registered entry, and many states have enacted exception clauses. Where a Bremen inmate-placement question arises, the national framework is the operative standard rather than any local rule.
tangentialFactors:
Prison administration and registry offices are competences of each German state, so the practice a trans visitor or resident encounters in Bremen is set by Bremen's own institutions standing under the national act, not by the practice of other states.

The placement of a neo-Nazi prisoner in a men's prison despite a legal gender change, reported on 16 July 2026, prompted Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch an initiative in the national upper chamber to tighten the Self-Determination Act. Any resulting tightening would bind Bremen's registry offices and prison administration as well; the initiative is a live turbulence in the framework Bremen administers.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking a legal gender marker change apply to Bremen's own registry offices, which process the self-declaration under the national act; the city-state has not legislated its own procedure or added requirements of its own.

Residents held in Bremen's prisons are placed under the national standard, since Bremen has enacted no placement statute; the outcome therefore turns on the general rule tying placement to legal gender and on the exception clauses available to state law.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bremen-specific enforcement record, incident, complaint or ordinance concerning trans people appears in the source inventory. Whether Bremen's registry offices publish processing times, refusal rates or guidance of their own is not sourced here.

The inventory's account of Bremen as one of the two original host cities of Germany's first Christopher Street Days in 1979, and the federal criminal-law history surrounding Section 175, is general LGB history with no trans-specific bearing and does not inform the assessment above.

National-layer matters, including partner recognition, federal criminal law, federal anti-discrimination provisions and national custody statistics, belong to the parent record and are not restated here.
